## What you will learn

- The three pillars of Hadoop: HDFS, MapReduce and YARN
- MapReduce with Python scripts, compared with Spark
- How Spark uses the Hadoop FileSystem API (and why `s3a://` works)
- A single-node HDFS with Spark and Pandas
- Hadoop today and the move to the cloud

---

## Where Hadoop came from

| Year | Milestone |
|-----|-------|
| 2003–04 | Google publishes the **GFS** and **MapReduce** papers |
| 2006 | Doug Cutting and Mike Cafarella create **Hadoop**, open source |
| 2012 | Hadoop 2 moves resource management into **YARN** |
| 2014 | **Spark** becomes a top-level Apache project: same model, in memory |
| Today | In the cloud, object storage and Kubernetes; on-premise, Hadoop is still in production |

The central idea: **hundreds of ordinary machines instead of one giant server**, accepting that some will always be failing.

---

## The three pillars

| Pillar | Role | Most common modern equivalent |
|-------|------|------------------------------|
| **HDFS** | Distributed file system | S3, GCS, ADLS |
| **YARN** | Cluster resource manager | Kubernetes, Databricks/EMR managers |
| **MapReduce** | Processing model and engine | Spark, Flink |

Around them, an ecosystem: **Hive** (its Metastore is still a common catalog), **HBase**, **Sqoop** (retired), **Oozie** (replaced by Airflow and similar) and **Parquet/ORC**, more used than ever.

---

## HDFS: blocks and replication

```
  sales.csv (300 MB) -> block A (128) | block B (128) | block C (44)

             NameNode ("sales.csv = A, B, C; A is on 1, 2, 4...")
                │
     ┌──────────┼──────────┬──────────┬──────────┐
  DataNode 1  DataNode 2  DataNode 3  DataNode 4  DataNode 5
  [A] [C]     [A] [B]     [B] [C]     [A] [C]     [B]
```

- **128 MB** blocks by default, **3 copies** on different machines
- If a DataNode dies, the NameNode has the missing copies recreated
- The client asks the NameNode where the blocks are, then **reads directly from the DataNodes**

---

## HDFS: limits that still matter

| Limit | Consequence |
|-------|-------------|
| Files are **write-once** (append only) | No UPDATE; hence Delta and Iceberg |
| NameNode keeps everything in memory (~150 bytes per file or block) | The **small files problem** |
| Storage and compute on the same machines | More disk means buying more CPU too |

**Data locality: move the code to the data.** Moving 1 TB over the network is slow; moving a 10 KB program is instant. Spark inherited this: see **Locality Level** in the Spark UI (`NODE_LOCAL`, `RACK_LOCAL`, `ANY`).

---

## The Hadoop FileSystem API

Spark never talks directly to the disk, HDFS or S3. The **URL scheme** picks the implementation.

```
     spark.read.parquet("<scheme>://path")
                    │
         Hadoop FileSystem API
                    │
    ┌───────┬───────┼──────────┬──────────┐
  file://  hdfs://  s3a://     gs://      abfs://
  local    HDFS     Amazon S3  Google     Azure
```

`hdfs://` works out of the box: PySpark ships the Hadoop client. `s3a://`, `gs://` and `abfs://` need their connector. Any Hadoop setting goes through the `spark.hadoop.*` prefix.

---

## Blocks and Spark partitions

| API | How it splits the input |
|-----|------------------------|
| `sc.textFile` (RDD) | Hadoop `InputFormat`: **one partition per block** |
| `spark.read` (DataFrame) | Its own criterion (`spark.sql.files.maxPartitionBytes`); blocks decide **where** tasks run |

```python
print(sc.textFile(CORPUS).getNumPartitions())
print(spark.read.text(CORPUS).rdd.getNumPartitions())
```

---

## MapReduce: the model

```
  MAP                     SHUFFLE & SORT           REDUCE
  "spark hdfs" -> (spark,1)(hdfs,1)    hdfs  -> [1,1] -> (hdfs, 2)
  "hdfs yarn"  -> (hdfs,1)(yarn,1) ──▶ spark -> [1,1] -> (spark, 2)
  "spark"      -> (spark,1)            yarn  -> [1]   -> (yarn, 1)
```

| Step | Who writes it | Parallelism |
|-----|--------------|-------------|
| Map | You | One task per input block |
| Shuffle & Sort | The framework | `hash(key) % R` chooses the reducer |
| Reduce | You | R tasks, with **sorted** keys |

The same as a Spark `groupBy`: map is the stage before the `Exchange`, reduce the stage after it.

---

## Hadoop Streaming: MapReduce in Python

Any program that reads stdin and writes stdout. You can test a whole job in the terminal:

```bash
cat input | python mapper.py | sort | python reducer.py
```

```python
# mapper.py
for line in sys.stdin:
    for word in re.findall(r"[a-z]+", line.lower()):
        print(f"{word}\t1")

# reducer.py: the input is sorted, so each key arrives together
current, count = None, 0
for line in sys.stdin:
    word, n = line.rstrip("\n").split("\t")
    if word != current:
        if current is not None:
            print(f"{current}\t{count}")
        current, count = word, 0
    count += int(n)
if current is not None:
    print(f"{current}\t{count}")
```

---

## The same word count in Spark

```python
# RDD: the original API, mimics map/reduce
(sc.textFile(CORPUS)
   .flatMap(lambda line: re.findall(r"[a-z]+", line.lower()))
   .map(lambda w: (w, 1))
   .reduceByKey(lambda a, b: a + b))

# DataFrame
(spark.read.text(CORPUS)
   .select(F.explode(F.split(F.lower("value"), " ")).alias("word"))
   .groupBy("word").count())
```

## Why Spark replaced MapReduce

```
  MapReduce: HDFS ─▶ [job 1] ─▶ HDFS ─▶ [job 2] ─▶ HDFS ─▶ ...
  Spark:     HDFS ─▶ [stage 1] ─shuffle─▶ [stage 2] ─▶ HDFS
```

| | MapReduce | Spark |
|-|-----------|-------|
| Between steps | Writes to HDFS (disk + replication) | Memory / local disk |
| Iterative algorithms | One job per iteration | Cached data between iterations |
| API | Only map and reduce | DataFrames, SQL, streaming, ML |
| Optimizer | None | Catalyst + AQE |

---

## YARN: who runs where

| YARN | Spark |
|------|-------|
| ResourceManager | The cluster's "master" |
| ApplicationMaster | In `cluster` mode, the driver runs inside it |
| Container | Each **executor** is one container |
| Queues | Limit how much each team can use |

On the Spark side, the main change is `--master` (`local[*]`, `yarn`, `k8s://...`, `spark://...`):

```bash
spark-submit --master yarn --deploy-mode cluster \
  --num-executors 10 --executor-cores 4 --executor-memory 8g \
  --queue analytics pipeline_silver.py
```

## Hands-on: single-node HDFS

NameNode and DataNode on one machine: the same software as a 1,000-node cluster.

```bash
hdfs namenode -format -force -nonInteractive
hdfs --daemon start namenode
hdfs --daemon start datanode

hdfs dfs -mkdir -p /aula9/raw
hdfs dfs -put -f corpus.txt /aula9/raw/corpus.txt
hdfs dfs -D dfs.blocksize=4194304 -put -f corpus.txt /aula9/raw/corpus_4mb.txt
hdfs dfs -ls -h /aula9/raw
hdfs fsck /aula9/raw/corpus_4mb.txt -files -blocks -locations
```

Blocks are plain `blk_<id>` files on the DataNode's disk. The NameNode never sees their content.

---

## Spark and Pandas on HDFS

```python
# Spark: HDFS is just another URL scheme
HDFS = "hdfs://localhost:9000"
words = (spark.read.text(f"{HDFS}/aula9/raw/corpus.txt")
         .select(F.explode(F.split("value", " ")).alias("word"))
         .groupBy("word").count())
words.write.mode("overwrite").parquet(f"{HDFS}/aula9/gold/wordcount")

# Pandas through PyArrow (libhdfs)
hdfs = pafs.HadoopFileSystem("localhost", 9000)
wc = pq.read_table("/aula9/gold/wordcount", filesystem=hdfs).to_pandas()

# Without libhdfs: WebHDFS, the REST API
requests.get("http://localhost:9870/webhdfs/v1/aula9/raw?op=LISTSTATUS").json()
```

The `_SUCCESS` marker means the output is complete. Spark writes it too, inherited from Hadoop.

## Hadoop today {.smaller}

The biggest change: **separating storage from compute**. Cheap object storage all the time; clusters that start and stop per job.

| Component | Status |
|-----------|--------|
| **HDFS** | Still strong on-premise; replaced by object storage in the cloud |
| **MapReduce** | Almost only in legacy systems |
| **YARN** | Still widely used (including AWS EMR); Kubernetes is growing fast |
| **FileSystem API** | **Everywhere**: how Spark, Hive, Trino and Flink reach S3/GCS/ADLS |
| **Parquet/ORC** | The analytical storage standard |

---

## Summary {.smaller}

| Concept | Hadoop | In Spark |
|---------|--------|----------|
| Distributed files | HDFS: 128 MB blocks, 3 replicas | `hdfs://` through the FileSystem API |
| Processing | MapReduce: map, shuffle and sort, reduce | Stages separated by shuffles |
| Resources | YARN: ResourceManager, containers | `--master yarn`, executors = containers |
| Code to the data | Block locality | `Locality Level` in the Spark UI |
| Output complete | `_SUCCESS` marker | The same marker |
| Settings | `core-site.xml`, `hdfs-site.xml` | `spark.hadoop.*` |
| Cloud | S3A, GCS, ABFS connectors | `s3a://`, `gs://`, `abfs://` |
